overview: Delta Live Tables (DLT), now branded as Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines, is a declarative ETL framework on Databricks where you describe the transformations you want (the target tables and their queries) and DLT manages the orchestration, dependency resolution, incremental processing, and infrastructure automatically.

Instead of writing imperative code that manually reads, writes, checkpoints, and orders tasks, you author @dlt.table / @dlt.view decorators (Python) or CREATE STREAMING TABLE / CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW statements (SQL), and DLT builds a dependency DAG, applies data quality expectations, and runs the pipeline with the correct execution semantics.

DLT is the backbone of the medallion architecture (bronze -> silver -> gold) on Databricks and integrates natively with Auto Loader, Structured Streaming, Unity Catalog, and CDC via APPLY CHANGES INTO, making it a frequent senior/staff interview and design topic.
learningObjectives: Explain the declarative pipeline paradigm and how DLT differs from hand-written Structured Streaming / Workflows jobs.
Distinguish streaming tables from materialized views and know when each is the right dataset type.
Apply data quality expectations (@dlt.expect, expect_or_drop, expect_or_fail, expect_all) and read expectation metrics from the DLT event log.
Implement CDC and SCD Type 1/Type 2 with APPLY CHANGES INTO, and configure pipeline settings (development vs production, triggered vs continuous, enhanced autoscaling) for production.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: Delta Live Tables (Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines) is a declarative framework for building reliable, maintainable, and testable data processing pipelines on the Databricks Lakehouse. You define datasets (streaming tables, materialized views, and temporary views) and their transformation logic; DLT infers the dependency graph from the queries, determines whether each dataset should be computed incrementally (streaming) or fully/incrementally recomputed (materialized view), enforces declarative data quality constraints called expectations, manages checkpoints and Delta table maintenance, and orchestrates execution in a managed pipeline runtime with automatic error handling, retries, and enhanced autoscaling.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of DLT as telling Databricks WHAT tables you want and HOW each one is computed from others, then letting the system figure out the order to run them, when to run them, how to only process new data, and how to catch bad records. You write the recipes; DLT is the head chef that sequences the kitchen, keeps the pantry (checkpoints) organized, and inspects the ingredients (data quality) before they reach the plate.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Databricks introduced Delta Live Tables in 2021 (GA in 2022) to solve the operational pain of hand-built Spark Structured Streaming pipelines, where engineers manually managed checkpoints, task ordering, backfills, schema evolution, and data quality. DLT abstracted that boilerplate behind a declarative API. Over time it gained APPLY CHANGES INTO for CDC/SCD, enhanced autoscaling, Unity Catalog integration, serverless pipelines, and the event log for observability. In 2025 Databricks rebranded DLT as Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines under the broader Lakeflow umbrella, and open-sourced the declarative core as Apache Spark Declarative Pipelines, while the @dlt APIs and SQL syntax remain the foundation.

whyItMatters.business: DLT dramatically reduces the time and specialized skill needed to ship reliable data pipelines, letting teams deliver fresh, trustworthy data products (dashboards, ML features, reports) faster while lowering the operational headcount required to keep pipelines running.
whyItMatters.engineering: Engineers stop writing checkpoint management, task DAGs, retry loops, and manual backfill logic; instead they declare tables and expectations. This removes entire classes of bugs (ordering, checkpoint corruption, forgotten data quality checks) and makes pipelines testable and reviewable as code.
whyItMatters.scalability: DLT with enhanced autoscaling automatically adds and removes workers based on streaming backlog and task load, and can process bounded (triggered) or unbounded (continuous) workloads across bronze/silver/gold layers without manual cluster tuning.
whyItMatters.cost: Enhanced autoscaling proactively scales down when the backlog clears, triggered pipelines spin compute up only when needed, and serverless DLT bills for actual usage, so teams pay for processing rather than idle long-running streaming clusters.
whyItMatters.reliability: Declarative dependencies, automatic checkpointing, exactly-once streaming semantics on Delta, expectations that quarantine or fail on bad data, and automatic retries make pipelines self-healing and auditable, which is essential for regulated and revenue-critical data.

coreComponents.name: Datasets: Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, and Views
coreComponents.definition: The three declarative dataset types DLT can produce: a streaming table (incrementally processes an append-only or streaming source), a materialized view (result of a query on batch data that DLT keeps up to date, incrementally when possible), and a (temporary) view used for intermediate logic not persisted as a table.
coreComponents.purpose: To let you declare the shape of each layer of the medallion architecture with the right freshness and recomputation semantics.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Streaming tables handle low-latency, append-heavy ingestion and are backed by Structured Streaming with managed checkpoints; materialized views handle aggregations/joins over full datasets and are refreshed incrementally by Enzyme when possible; views compute on read and are not materialized.
coreComponents.examples: @dlt.table decorating a function that returns spark.readStream (streaming table); @dlt.table over a batch aggregation (materialized view); @dlt.view for a reusable filter; SQL CREATE STREAMING TABLE and CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW.

coreComponents.name: Expectations (Data Quality Constraints)
coreComponents.definition: Declarative data quality rules applied to a dataset via @dlt.expect (log/track), @dlt.expect_or_drop (drop failing rows), @dlt.expect_or_fail (fail the pipeline update), and @dlt.expect_all / @dlt.expect_all_or_drop / @dlt.expect_all_or_fail for multiple rules, or SQL CONSTRAINT ... EXPECT (...) ON VIOLATION clauses.
coreComponents.purpose: To validate data as it flows through the pipeline and to record quality metrics without writing separate validation jobs.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Evaluate boolean conditions per row, take the configured action (retain-and-report, drop, or fail), and emit pass/fail counts into the DLT event log for monitoring and alerting.
coreComponents.examples: @dlt.expect_or_drop("valid_id", "id IS NOT NULL"); CONSTRAINT positive_amount EXPECT (amount > 0) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW; expectation metrics queried from the event_log.

coreComponents.name: Pipeline Runtime and Configuration
coreComponents.definition: The managed DLT execution environment that reads the pipeline settings (target catalog/schema, development vs production mode, triggered vs continuous execution, cluster/serverless config, enhanced autoscaling) and orchestrates the DAG.
coreComponents.purpose: To run the declared datasets in the correct dependency order with the right latency and resource model, and to manage retries, checkpoints, and table maintenance.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Resolve the dependency graph from dlt.read/read_stream references, provision compute (classic or serverless) with autoscaling, run in development (fast iteration, cluster reuse, no auto-retry) or production (retries, fresh clusters) mode, and publish datasets to the configured Unity Catalog catalog.schema.
coreComponents.examples: Setting continuous=false for triggered runs; enabling Enhanced Autoscaling; specifying target catalog 'main' and schema 'sales'; toggling development mode in the pipeline UI or JSON settings.

coreComponents.name: APPLY CHANGES INTO (CDC / SCD Engine)
coreComponents.definition: A declarative construct (dlt.apply_changes in Python, APPLY CHANGES INTO in SQL) that ingests change data capture feeds and maintains a target table as SCD Type 1 (overwrite) or Type 2 (history-preserving) using specified key, sequence, and optional apply-as-delete columns.
coreComponents.purpose: To handle out-of-order CDC records and merge them into a slowly changing dimension without hand-writing MERGE logic and ordering.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Deduplicate and order changes by the sequence column, apply inserts/updates/deletes, and, for Type 2, maintain __START_AT/__END_AT (or specified) validity columns to preserve history.
coreComponents.examples: dlt.apply_changes(target="customers", source="customers_cdc", keys=["id"], sequence_by="seq", stored_as_scd_type=2); SQL APPLY CHANGES INTO live.customers FROM stream(live.cdc) KEYS (id) SEQUENCE BY seq STORED AS SCD TYPE 2.

coreComponents.name: DLT Event Log
coreComponents.definition: An append-only Delta table (queryable via the event_log() table-valued function or a published event_log table) that records every pipeline event: dataset completion, expectation metrics, flow progress, autoscaling decisions, lineage, and errors.
coreComponents.purpose: To provide observability, auditability, and data-quality monitoring for pipeline runs.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Capture structured events with details (row counts, expectation pass/fail, dropped records, cluster events) that can be queried with SQL for dashboards and alerting.
coreComponents.examples: SELECT * FROM event_log(pipeline_id) WHERE event_type = 'flow_progress'; extracting details:flow_progress.data_quality.expectations to build a data-quality dashboard.

internalWorking: When a pipeline update starts, DLT parses all dataset definitions (Python decorators or SQL statements), and resolves inter-dataset references (dlt.read, dlt.read_stream, spark.readStream.table, LIVE./STREAM() references) to build a directed acyclic graph of datasets.

DLT classifies each dataset as a streaming table (backed by Structured Streaming with a system-managed checkpoint) or a materialized view (backed by a Delta table refreshed by the Enzyme incremental engine), then plans the execution order topologically so upstream datasets complete before dependents.

For streaming tables, DLT manages checkpoints, offsets, and exactly-once semantics automatically; for materialized views, Enzyme decides whether an incremental refresh (using change data and prior results) or a full recompute is cheaper.

Expectations are compiled into per-row predicates evaluated during the transformation; based on the action (track, drop, or fail) DLT records metrics to the event log and either keeps, filters, or aborts the update.

APPLY CHANGES INTO stages the source changes, orders them by the sequence column, and performs an internal MERGE into the target with SCD Type 1 or Type 2 semantics, transparently handling late/out-of-order records.
Throughout the run, enhanced autoscaling monitors streaming backlog and task queue depth to add or remove executors, and all progress, metrics, and errors are streamed to the DLT event log.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Source (cloud files / Kafka / Delta CDC) -> Auto Loader / readStream -> Bronze streaming table (@dlt.table + expectations) -> dlt.read_stream / dlt.read -> Silver streaming table or materialized view (cleansing, APPLY CHANGES for CDC) -> Gold materialized view (aggregations) -> Unity Catalog target catalog.schema -> Event Log (observability) -> BI / ML consumers
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. Raw files land in cloud storage; a bronze @dlt.table function uses spark.readStream.format('cloudFiles') (Auto Loader) to incrementally ingest them, attaching expectations to tag malformed records.
2. DLT resolves that a silver dataset reads from the bronze table via dlt.read_stream('bronze'), so it schedules bronze before silver in the DAG.
3. The silver streaming table cleanses and conforms data, applying @dlt.expect_or_drop to remove rows with null keys, and DLT records how many rows were dropped in the event log.
4. If the source is a CDC feed, dlt.apply_changes (or APPLY CHANGES INTO) merges ordered changes into a silver dimension as SCD Type 2, maintaining validity columns.
5. A gold materialized view aggregates the conformed silver data (e.g., daily revenue); Enzyme refreshes it incrementally when only new/changed rows arrive.
6. All datasets are published to the configured Unity Catalog catalog.schema, and every flow's progress, row counts, and expectation metrics are written to the DLT event log for monitoring.

keyTerminology.meaning: A Delta table declared in DLT that incrementally processes data from a streaming or append-only source using Structured Streaming with DLT-managed checkpoints; each input row is processed exactly once.
keyTerminology.importance: It is the correct type for low-latency ingestion (bronze) and append-heavy transformations; misusing a materialized view here forces expensive recomputation.

keyTerminology.meaning: A DLT dataset whose results are computed from a (typically batch) query and kept up to date by the Enzyme incremental refresh engine, recomputing only what changed when possible.
keyTerminology.importance: It is ideal for aggregations, joins, and gold-layer serving tables where correctness over the full dataset matters and freshness can lag ingestion.

keyTerminology.meaning: A declarative data quality constraint (a named boolean condition) with an action of retain-and-report, drop, or fail, evaluated on rows flowing into a dataset.
keyTerminology.importance: Expectations move data quality into the pipeline definition itself, producing auditable metrics instead of separate, drift-prone validation jobs.

keyTerminology.meaning: The DLT CDC construct that merges an ordered change feed into a target table as SCD Type 1 or Type 2, handling out-of-order records via a sequence column.
keyTerminology.importance: It replaces fragile hand-written MERGE-and-order logic and is the standard way to build dimensions from CDC in DLT.

keyTerminology.meaning: An append-only Delta table capturing all pipeline events, expectation metrics, lineage, and cluster/autoscaling activity for a pipeline.
keyTerminology.importance: It is the single source of truth for observing pipeline health, data quality trends, and lineage, and is the basis for alerting and dashboards.

importantConcepts.explanation: In imperative Structured Streaming or Workflows, you write the exact sequence of reads, transforms, writes, checkpoints, and task dependencies. In DLT you declare each target dataset and its query; DLT derives the DAG, execution order, incrementalization, and checkpoint management. This shifts you from telling the system HOW to run to declaring WHAT should exist, reducing boilerplate and ordering bugs.

Development mode reuses the cluster across runs for fast iteration and disables automatic retries so errors surface immediately, ideal while building. Production mode terminates and recreates clusters per run, enables automatic retry with backoff on retryable failures, and is intended for scheduled, reliable operation. The mode is a pipeline setting toggled in the UI or JSON and does not change your dataset code.

variationsAndTypes: **Triggered pipelines:** Run once (or on a schedule), process all currently available data, then stop the compute; cost-efficient for periodic batch/near-batch workloads.
**Continuous pipelines:** Keep running to process data with low latency as it arrives; best for always-on streaming SLAs at higher steady-state cost.
**Serverless DLT pipelines:** Databricks manages the compute entirely, with fast startup and usage-based billing, and unlocks features like Enzyme-optimized materialized views.
**Classic (customer-compute) DLT pipelines:** Run on DLT-managed clusters in your compute with configurable node types and enhanced autoscaling.

**Python (@dlt) pipelines vs. SQL pipelines:** Python offers programmatic table generation and UDFs; SQL offers CREATE STREAMING TABLE / MATERIALIZED VIEW / APPLY CHANGES for analysts, and both can be mixed within one pipeline.
advantages: **Less boilerplate, fewer bugs:** DLT manages checkpoints, task ordering, retries, and backfills, eliminating whole classes of streaming errors.
**Built-in data quality:** Expectations and event-log metrics make quality a first-class, auditable part of the pipeline.
**Automatic dependency management:** The DAG is inferred from queries, so refactoring dependencies just works without manual rewiring.
**Native CDC/SCD support:** APPLY CHANGES INTO handles out-of-order changes and Type 1/2 dimensions declaratively.
**Enhanced autoscaling and serverless:** Compute scales to backlog and can bill per use, optimizing cost and latency without manual tuning.
disadvantages: **Framework lock-in and abstraction limits:** Some highly custom streaming patterns (arbitrary stateful operations, complex foreachBatch sinks) are harder or unsupported within DLT's model.
**Cost of continuous mode:** Always-on continuous pipelines keep compute running, which can be expensive if latency requirements do not truly demand it.
**Learning curve on semantics:** Choosing streaming table vs. materialized view, and understanding incremental refresh limits, requires understanding DLT internals.
**Debugging indirection:** Because DLT manages execution, diagnosing failures means reading the event log and pipeline UI rather than plain driver logs.
**Some sinks/features gated:** Certain sink types, external writes, or older runtime features may not be available inside DLT and require standard jobs.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use DLT for medallion-architecture ETL/ELT where you want managed incremental processing, built-in data quality, CDC/SCD dimensions, and low operational overhead, especially multi-hop bronze/silver/gold pipelines feeding BI and ML.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid DLT for one-off ad-hoc transforms, workloads needing arbitrary custom stateful streaming or unsupported sinks, or when tight low-level control over Spark execution and checkpoints is required, where plain Structured Streaming or Workflows fits better.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: DLT is like a modern smart factory assembly line: you specify each station's job and the quality checks (expectations), and the factory management system figures out the order of stations, moves parts (data) between them, only reworks the parts that changed (incremental refresh), pulls defective parts off the line (drop/fail), scales the number of workers to demand (autoscaling), and keeps a detailed production log (event log). You design the stations; the factory runs itself.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A materialized view in DLT always fully recomputes from scratch on every run.
commonMisconceptions.reality: DLT's Enzyme engine performs incremental refresh when it can (using change data and prior results), only falling back to full recompute when the query pattern or source changes make incremental impossible.

commonMisconceptions.myth: @dlt.expect drops or blocks bad rows by default.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Plain @dlt.expect only tracks and reports violations (rows are retained); you must use expect_or_drop to remove failing rows or expect_or_fail to abort the update on violations.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Enable enhanced autoscaling so DLT scales workers based on streaming backlog and task load, and use streaming tables for high-throughput ingestion with Auto Loader; partition and cluster gold tables appropriately. Serverless DLT further removes cluster sizing decisions.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Run production pipelines in production mode for automatic retries and fresh clusters; streaming tables provide exactly-once processing via managed checkpoints, and Delta ACID transactions ensure consistent commits even on failure.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: DLT automatically checkpoints streaming state and retries retryable failures; idempotent Delta writes and APPLY CHANGES ordering ensure re-runs do not duplicate or corrupt data. Failed updates roll back atomically at the dataset level.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Query the DLT event log (event_log() TVF or published event_log table) for flow_progress, expectation metrics, and cluster events; use the pipeline UI DAG and metrics, and build dashboards on expectation pass/fail rates.
productionConsiderations.security: Publish datasets to Unity Catalog (target catalog and schema) so access is governed by UC grants, lineage is tracked, and pipelines run under a defined service principal/run-as identity with least-privilege access to sources and targets.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Prefer triggered execution for periodic workloads, use enhanced autoscaling and serverless to avoid idle compute, right-size node types, and use materialized views with incremental refresh to avoid recomputing unchanged aggregates.
productionConsiderations.performance: Use Auto Loader for efficient incremental file discovery, keep bronze minimal (schema-on-read, light validation), push heavy joins/aggregations to silver/gold, and rely on Enzyme incremental refresh and Photon-enabled compute for gold-layer serving performance.

codeExamples.title: Bronze ingestion with Auto Loader and expectations (Python @dlt)
codeExamples.overview: A bronze streaming table that incrementally ingests JSON files from cloud storage using Auto Loader (cloudFiles) and tags malformed records with an expectation that only tracks (does not drop).
codeExamples.breakdown: @dlt.table declares a streaming table (because the function returns spark.readStream). Auto Loader's cloudFiles source incrementally discovers new JSON files and evolves schema using the schemaLocation. @dlt.expect('has_order_id', ...) records how many rows violate the rule in the event log but retains them. DLT manages the checkpoint automatically; you never specify one.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A Delta streaming table main.sales.bronze_orders that grows as new files arrive, with an _ingested_at column and expectation metrics (pass/fail counts for has_order_id) visible in the pipeline UI and event log.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting cloudFiles.schemaLocation causes schema inference errors; pointing load() at a non-Volume path without proper UC access fails; expecting @dlt.expect to drop rows (it only tracks).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Keep bronze transformations minimal; use cloudFiles.inferColumnTypes only for JSON/CSV and pin schemas once stable; set cloudFiles.maxFilesPerTrigger to control batch size and backlog.

codeExamples.title: Silver cleansing with drop/fail expectations reading the bronze table
codeExamples.overview: A silver streaming table that reads the bronze table with dlt.read_stream, cleanses data, and applies multiple expectations with expect_all_or_drop to remove invalid rows and one expect_or_fail for a critical invariant.
codeExamples.breakdown: dlt.read_stream('bronze_orders') creates a streaming dependency on the bronze table, so DLT runs bronze first. expect_all_or_drop evaluates all three named rules and drops any row failing any of them (recording drop counts). expect_or_fail('valid_currency', ...) aborts the entire update if any row has an unexpected currency, protecting a hard business invariant.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A streaming table main.sales.silver_orders containing only rows that passed the drop rules, with the pipeline failing loudly if any unexpected currency appears; event log shows dropped-row counts per expectation.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Using dlt.read (batch) instead of dlt.read_stream breaks incremental semantics; an over-strict expect_or_fail can halt production repeatedly; casting errors if amount is non-numeric text.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Reserve expect_or_fail for true invariants; use expect_or_drop with a quarantine table for triage; keep silver deterministic and idempotent so retries are safe.

codeExamples.title: Gold aggregation as a materialized view
codeExamples.overview: A gold materialized view that aggregates conformed silver data into daily revenue per currency; DLT (Enzyme) refreshes it incrementally when possible.
codeExamples.breakdown: Because the function uses dlt.read (batch read of the full table) and an aggregation, DLT treats gold_daily_revenue as a materialized view. When silver_orders changes, Enzyme attempts an incremental refresh of the aggregate rather than a full scan. The result is a serving-ready gold table governed by Unity Catalog.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A materialized view main.sales.gold_daily_revenue with one row per (order_date, currency) holding total_revenue and order_count, kept fresh as silver grows.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Using dlt.read_stream for an aggregation that needs the full dataset produces incorrect running results; non-incrementalizable query patterns force full recompute and higher cost.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Keep aggregation queries incremental-friendly (avoid non-deterministic or full-window functions where possible), run on serverless to leverage Enzyme, and enable Photon for fast aggregation.

codeExamples.title: SQL pipeline: streaming table, materialized view, and expectations
codeExamples.overview: The equivalent bronze/silver/gold layers expressed in DLT SQL syntax with CREATE STREAMING TABLE, CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW, and CONSTRAINT ... EXPECT clauses.
codeExamples.code:
-- Bronze: streaming ingest via Auto Loader
CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE bronze_orders
  COMMENT "Raw orders via Auto Loader"
  TBLPROPERTIES ("quality" = "bronze")
AS SELECT *, current_timestamp() AS _ingested_at
FROM STREAM read_files(
  '/Volumes/main/sales/landing/orders/',
  format => 'json'
);

-- Silver: cleansed streaming table with expectations
CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE silver_orders (
  CONSTRAINT valid_order_id EXPECT (order_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW,
  CONSTRAINT valid_currency EXPECT (currency IN ('USD','EUR','GBP')) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE
)
  COMMENT "Cleansed orders"
AS SELECT order_id, customer_id, CAST(amount AS DOUBLE) AS amount, currency,
          to_date(order_ts) AS order_date
FROM STREAM(live.bronze_orders);

-- Gold: materialized view aggregation
CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW gold_daily_revenue
  COMMENT "Daily revenue by currency"
AS SELECT order_date, currency,
          SUM(amount) AS total_revenue,
          COUNT(order_id) AS order_count
FROM live.silver_orders
GROUP BY order_date, currency;
codeExamples.breakdown: CREATE STREAMING TABLE with STREAM read_files(...) uses Auto Loader for incremental ingest. The CONSTRAINT ... EXPECT clauses inline the expectations: DROP ROW filters violators, FAIL UPDATE aborts the run. STREAM(live.bronze_orders) declares a streaming dependency; live.silver_orders (batch) plus GROUP BY makes gold a materialized view refreshed incrementally.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Three published datasets in the pipeline's target catalog.schema mirroring the Python example, with expectation metrics in the event log.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Omitting STREAM() around a source turns a streaming dependency into batch; mixing OR REFRESH semantics incorrectly; referencing tables without the live. prefix inside a DLT pipeline.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use CREATE OR REFRESH so re-deploys are idempotent; keep constraints named for clear event-log metrics; use read_files for modern Auto Loader ingestion in SQL.

codeExamples.title: CDC to SCD Type 2 with APPLY CHANGES INTO
codeExamples.overview: Building a slowly changing dimension (Type 2, history-preserving) from a CDC change feed using dlt.apply_changes in Python and the SQL equivalent.
codeExamples.code:
import dlt

# 1) Bronze streaming table capturing the raw CDC feed
@dlt.table(name="customers_cdc")
def customers_cdc():
    return spark.readStream.table("main.raw.customers_change_feed")

# 2) Target dimension maintained as SCD Type 2
dlt.create_streaming_table("customers_scd2")

dlt.apply_changes(
    target="customers_scd2",
    source="customers_cdc",
    keys=["customer_id"],
    sequence_by="change_seq",
    apply_as_deletes="operation = 'DELETE'",
    except_column_list=["operation", "change_seq"],
    stored_as_scd_type=2
)

# SQL equivalent:
# CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE customers_scd2;
# APPLY CHANGES INTO live.customers_scd2
#   FROM STREAM(live.customers_cdc)
#   KEYS (customer_id)
#   APPLY AS DELETE WHEN operation = 'DELETE'
#   SEQUENCE BY change_seq
#   COLUMNS * EXCEPT (operation, change_seq)
#   STORED AS SCD TYPE 2;
codeExamples.breakdown: dlt.create_streaming_table declares the empty target. dlt.apply_changes reads the ordered CDC source, uses customer_id as the key and change_seq to order out-of-order records, treats operation='DELETE' rows as deletes, excludes control columns, and maintains SCD Type 2 history with automatically managed __START_AT/__END_AT validity columns. The SQL APPLY CHANGES INTO is the direct equivalent.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A dimension table customers_scd2 where each customer_id can have multiple rows across time, current row(s) having an open end date, correctly reflecting inserts, updates, and deletes regardless of arrival order.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Wrong sequence_by leads to incorrect ordering and lost updates; forgetting apply_as_deletes leaves stale rows; using SCD Type 1 when history is needed; not excluding operation/seq control columns.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Choose a monotonic sequence column (LSN, commit timestamp); use SCD Type 1 when only current state is needed to save storage; keep the CDC bronze table lean and let APPLY CHANGES handle dedup/ordering.

codeExamples.title: Querying the DLT event log for data-quality and pipeline health
codeExamples.overview: Extracting expectation pass/fail metrics and flow progress from the DLT event log to power a data-quality dashboard.
codeExamples.code:
-- Expectation metrics from flow_progress events
SELECT
  timestamp,
  details:flow_progress.status                         AS status,
  explode_outer(from_json(
    details:flow_progress.data_quality.expectations,
    'array<struct<name:string,dataset:string,passed_records:long,failed_records:long>>'
  ))                                                    AS expectation
FROM event_log("<pipeline_id>")
WHERE event_type = 'flow_progress'
  AND details:flow_progress.data_quality.expectations IS NOT NULL;

-- Latest completion status per dataset
SELECT details:flow_definition.output_dataset AS dataset,
       details:flow_progress.status           AS status,
       max(timestamp)                          AS last_seen
FROM event_log("<pipeline_id>")
WHERE event_type = 'flow_progress'
GROUP BY 1, 2;
codeExamples.breakdown: event_log('<pipeline_id>') is a table-valued function exposing the pipeline's structured events. flow_progress events carry data_quality.expectations JSON with per-expectation passed/failed record counts, parsed with from_json and explode_outer. This lets you trend data quality and detect failing datasets without leaving SQL.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Rows of expectation names with passed_records/failed_records per run, plus latest status per dataset, suitable for a Databricks SQL dashboard or alert.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Using the wrong pipeline_id; not accounting for the event log being published to a UC schema when target is set; schema of details JSON varying by event_type.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Publish the event log to a stable UC table for long-term trending; build a materialized view over expectation metrics; alert when failed_records exceeds a threshold.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A subscription streaming service needs a reliable near-real-time pipeline that ingests raw playback and billing events, cleanses them, maintains an accurate customer dimension from a CDC feed, and serves daily revenue and engagement metrics to BI, all with enforced data quality and minimal operational overhead.
endToEndExample.inputData: Semi-structured JSON playback/billing events landing continuously in a Unity Catalog Volume, plus a Debezium-style CDC change feed for the customer master data delivered as a Delta table.
endToEndExample.architecture: A single DLT (Lakeflow Declarative) pipeline implementing medallion: bronze streaming tables ingest events via Auto Loader (read_files/cloudFiles) and the CDC feed; silver streaming tables cleanse events with expectations and APPLY CHANGES INTO builds an SCD Type 2 customer dimension; a gold materialized view aggregates daily revenue and engagement. The pipeline targets Unity Catalog catalog 'main', schema 'streaming_analytics', runs in production mode with enhanced autoscaling on serverless compute, triggered on an hourly schedule.
processingSteps: 1. Bronze: @dlt.table functions ingest playback/billing JSON via Auto Loader and the customer CDC feed via spark.readStream.table, attaching @dlt.expect to tag missing IDs.
2. Silver events: dlt.read_stream of bronze events with @dlt.expect_all_or_drop removing null-key/negative-amount rows and @dlt.expect_or_fail guarding valid currencies.
3. Silver dimension: dlt.apply_changes merges the CDC feed into customers_scd2 as SCD Type 2, ordered by commit sequence, handling deletes.
4. Gold: a materialized view joins silver events to the current customer rows and aggregates daily revenue and watch-time, refreshed incrementally by Enzyme.
5. All datasets publish to main.streaming_analytics in Unity Catalog; the DLT event log captures row counts, expectation metrics, and autoscaling events.
endToEndExample.output: Governed Delta datasets in main.streaming_analytics: bronze raw tables, cleansed silver event tables, a Type 2 customer dimension, and a gold daily revenue/engagement materialized view consumed by Databricks SQL dashboards.
endToEndExample.monitoring: A Databricks SQL dashboard queries event_log() for expectation pass/fail trends, dropped-row counts, and per-dataset completion status; alerts fire when failed_records exceeds thresholds or a flow enters FAILED status.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Production mode retries retryable failures with backoff; expect_or_drop quarantines bad rows while expect_or_fail halts on invariant violations; Delta ACID and managed checkpoints guarantee exactly-once, atomic commits so retries never duplicate data.
endToEndExample.finalResult: The team ships a self-managing, hourly-refreshed medallion pipeline with enforced data quality and a correct historical customer dimension, replacing hundreds of lines of hand-written streaming/checkpoint/MERGE code with declarative definitions and gaining full observability via the event log.

industryUseCases.problem: Dozens of source systems emit order, inventory, and clickstream data that must be ingested, cleansed, and modeled into consistent gold tables for merchandising and finance, with strict data quality and freshness SLAs.
industryUseCases.solution: A DLT medallion pipeline uses Auto Loader for bronze ingestion, expectations to enforce quality at silver, APPLY CHANGES INTO to maintain product and customer dimensions from CDC, and gold materialized views for reporting, all governed by Unity Catalog.
industryUseCases.benefits: Eliminated fragile hand-built streaming jobs, cut pipeline maintenance effort, gained auditable data-quality metrics, and reduced compute cost via enhanced autoscaling and triggered runs.

industryUseCases.problem: Regulatory reporting requires auditable, high-quality transformations of transaction data with full lineage and history-preserving dimensions for accounts and customers.
industryUseCases.solution: DLT pipelines ingest transactions via streaming tables with expect_or_fail on critical invariants, build SCD Type 2 dimensions with APPLY CHANGES INTO, and publish to Unity Catalog for governed access and lineage, with the event log providing audit evidence.
industryUseCases.benefits: Provable data quality and lineage for auditors, history preserved for point-in-time reporting, and reduced risk from removing manual MERGE/checkpoint code.

industryUseCases.problem: Millions of sensor readings per hour must be ingested with low latency, cleaned of malformed telemetry, and aggregated into equipment health and OEE metrics.
industryUseCases.solution: Continuous DLT streaming tables ingest telemetry via Auto Loader, expectations drop malformed readings and quarantine anomalies, and gold materialized views compute rolling equipment metrics with enhanced autoscaling handling bursty loads.
industryUseCases.benefits: Low-latency, self-scaling ingestion; automatic handling of backlog spikes; and reliable, quality-checked metrics feeding predictive maintenance without a large streaming ops team.

industryUseCases.problem: Clinical and claims feeds arrive from many partners with inconsistent quality and must be conformed into governed, high-integrity datasets for analytics while protecting PHI.
industryUseCases.solution: DLT pipelines enforce expectations for required fields and valid code sets, route violations to quarantine tables, maintain patient/provider dimensions with APPLY CHANGES INTO, and publish to Unity Catalog with fine-grained access controls.
industryUseCases.benefits: Consistent, quality-validated clinical datasets, PHI governed by Unity Catalog, and a clear audit trail of data-quality outcomes via the event log.

productionDeepDive.scalability: DLT scales horizontally with enhanced autoscaling, adding executors when streaming backlog or task load grows and proactively releasing them when the backlog clears. Streaming tables with Auto Loader efficiently discover and process large file volumes, while serverless DLT removes cluster sizing entirely and Enzyme incremental refresh keeps gold aggregations cheap at scale.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Streaming tables use DLT-managed checkpoints and Delta ACID transactions for exactly-once, atomic commits; failed updates roll back at the dataset level so partial writes never corrupt tables. APPLY CHANGES ordering and idempotent Delta writes ensure re-runs and retries do not duplicate data.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Managed DLT compute (especially serverless) restarts and reschedules on infrastructure failures; production mode provisions fresh clusters per run and retries retryable errors. Spreading classic compute across availability zones and relying on Delta storage durability protects against zone/instance loss.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Pipeline definitions live as code (notebooks/files in Git via Databricks Repos or asset bundles) and settings as JSON/Terraform, so a pipeline can be recreated in another workspace/region; Delta tables in cloud storage are replicated, and the event log provides an auditable recovery record.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Keep bronze thin (light validation), push heavy joins/aggregations to silver/gold, use Auto Loader for incremental discovery, prefer materialized views with incremental refresh for aggregates, enable Photon, and use liquid clustering / Z-ordering on gold serving tables for fast reads.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Use triggered pipelines for periodic workloads to avoid idle compute, enable enhanced autoscaling to scale to zero-work quickly, adopt serverless usage-based billing, and rely on Enzyme incremental refresh so unchanged aggregates are not recomputed. Right-size node types for classic compute.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Publish to Unity Catalog (target catalog and schema) so grants, row/column masking, and lineage apply; run pipelines under a least-privilege service principal (run-as); store source credentials in secrets; and restrict access to the event log and source Volumes via UC.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: The DLT event log is the primary observability surface: query flow_progress for status and row counts, data_quality.expectations for pass/fail/dropped metrics, and cluster/autoscaling events for capacity. The pipeline UI shows the live DAG, per-dataset metrics, and update history; integrate with alerting on failures and quality regressions.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Expectations are the built-in quality layer: expect (track), expect_or_drop (filter and quarantine), expect_or_fail (halt on invariant breaches), and expect_all variants for grouped rules. Metrics are emitted per expectation to the event log, enabling trend dashboards and automated alerts on rising failure rates.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Configure pipeline failure notifications (email/webhook), build Databricks SQL alerts over event-log expectation metrics, and export event-log data to a central observability/SIEM system. Alert on FAILED flows, expect_or_fail aborts, and dropped-row spikes indicating upstream quality regressions.

recommendedPractices: **Follow the medallion architecture:** keep bronze raw and minimal, cleanse and conform in silver with expectations, and model serving aggregates in gold.
**Choose dataset types deliberately:** streaming tables for append/ingest and materialized views for aggregations, matching freshness and cost to the layer.
**Enforce data quality with the right action:** track with expect, quarantine with expect_or_drop, and reserve expect_or_fail for true invariants.
**Use APPLY CHANGES INTO for CDC/SCD** rather than hand-written MERGE, choosing a reliable monotonic sequence column.
engineeringStandards: All production pipelines run in production mode with enhanced autoscaling and are deployed as code via Databricks Asset Bundles or Terraform.
Every dataset must carry a comment, quality table property, and at least one expectation where meaningful.
Pipelines must target a Unity Catalog catalog and schema; no unmanaged/hive_metastore targets in production.
designRecommendations: Reference upstream datasets via dlt.read_stream/dlt.read (or STREAM()/live. in SQL) so DLT infers the DAG; never bypass with direct paths.
Keep transformations deterministic and idempotent so retries and incremental refresh are safe.
Separate ingestion (bronze), conformance (silver), and serving (gold) into distinct datasets rather than one monolithic query.
namingConventions: Prefix datasets by layer and domain (bronze_orders, silver_orders, gold_daily_revenue).
Name expectations descriptively for readable event-log metrics (valid_order_id, positive_amount).
Name pipelines by domain and environment (sales_medallion_prod).
documentationStandards: Document each dataset's purpose and grain in its comment and in the pipeline README.
Document expectation intent and the chosen action (track/drop/fail) and any quarantine strategy.
Document the CDC sequence column, key columns, and SCD type chosen for each dimension.
testingStrategies: Develop in development mode for fast iteration, then validate in production mode before scheduling.
Assert data-quality outcomes by querying event-log expectation metrics in CI against sample data.
Test CDC/SCD logic with out-of-order and delete records to verify ordering and history correctness.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using @dlt.expect (track-only) and assuming bad rows are removed.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Confusing the three expectation actions; the plain expect only logs violations.
commonMistakes.impact: Invalid rows flow downstream and corrupt silver/gold results while metrics falsely suggest quality is enforced.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use expect_or_drop to filter (optionally with a quarantine table) or expect_or_fail to halt on invariant violations; reserve plain expect for observability-only rules.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing a materialized view where a streaming table is needed (or vice versa).
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Not understanding streaming (incremental append) vs. materialized (full/incremental recompute) semantics.
commonMistakes.impact: Streaming aggregations produce wrong running totals, or high-throughput ingest as a materialized view causes expensive full recomputes and latency.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use streaming tables (spark.readStream / dlt.read_stream) for append-heavy ingest and materialized views (dlt.read + aggregation) for full-dataset aggregates.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bypassing DLT dependency resolution by reading source paths directly instead of dlt.read/dlt.read_stream.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Copy-pasting standard Spark code that reads by path or table name outside the DLT graph.
commonMistakes.impact: DLT cannot infer the DAG, so ordering, incremental processing, and lineage break, leading to stale or incorrect results.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Reference upstream DLT datasets via dlt.read/dlt.read_stream (Python) or STREAM()/live. (SQL) so DLT builds and orders the dependency graph.

commonMistakes.mistake: Running continuous pipelines when latency does not require it.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Defaulting to continuous mode for a sense of freshness without evaluating SLAs.
commonMistakes.impact: Compute runs 24/7, inflating cost with little business benefit over triggered runs.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use triggered pipelines on a schedule for periodic needs; reserve continuous mode for genuine low-latency SLAs, and pair either with enhanced autoscaling.

commonMistakes.mistake: Picking a poor or non-monotonic sequence_by column for APPLY CHANGES INTO.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Using an arbitrary timestamp or column that can tie or go backwards across CDC batches.
commonMistakes.impact: Out-of-order records are applied incorrectly, causing lost updates or wrong SCD history.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use a reliable monotonic sequence such as a database LSN or commit version; validate ordering with out-of-order test cases.

comparisonSection.explanation: DLT lets you declare target datasets and queries while it manages the DAG, checkpoints, retries, and incrementalization. Imperative Structured Streaming with Workflows gives full low-level control but requires you to write checkpoints, task ordering, backfills, and data-quality checks yourself.

Materialized views compute over the full dataset and are refreshed incrementally by Enzyme, correct for aggregations/joins. Streaming tables process append-only input incrementally and are correct for ingestion and row-level transforms, not for full-dataset aggregates.

expect_or_drop removes violating rows and records drop counts, keeping the pipeline running (ideal for messy sources); expect_or_fail aborts the entire update on any violation, appropriate only for hard invariants where bad data must never pass.

Triggered processes all available data then stops compute (cost-efficient, higher latency); continuous keeps running for low-latency processing (higher steady-state cost). Choose based on freshness SLAs, both benefit from enhanced autoscaling.

comparisonSection.optionB: Manual MERGE INTO in a job
comparisonSection.explanation: APPLY CHANGES INTO declaratively handles ordering, dedup, deletes, and SCD Type 1/2 history. A manual MERGE requires you to code ordering, deduplication, and validity-column maintenance yourself, which is error-prone with out-of-order CDC.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is Delta Live Tables and how is it different from a normal Spark job?
beginnerQuestions.answer: DLT (Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines) is a declarative ETL framework where you define target datasets (streaming tables, materialized views, views) and their transformation queries, and DLT manages the dependency DAG, checkpoints, incremental processing, retries, and data quality. A normal Spark/Structured Streaming job is imperative: you manually write reads, writes, checkpoints, and orchestration.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: The key contrast is declarative (WHAT) vs. imperative (HOW); DLT removes boilerplate and infers ordering.

beginnerQuestions.question: What are the main dataset types in DLT?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Streaming tables (incrementally process append-only/streaming sources with managed checkpoints), materialized views (query results kept fresh via incremental refresh), and temporary views (compute-on-read, not persisted).
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Choosing the right type per medallion layer is fundamental, streaming for ingest, materialized views for aggregations.

intermediateQuestions.question: Explain the difference between @dlt.expect, expect_or_drop, and expect_or_fail.
intermediateQuestions.answer: @dlt.expect tracks violations and records metrics but retains the rows. @dlt.expect_or_drop removes rows that fail the condition (recording drop counts). @dlt.expect_or_fail aborts the entire pipeline update if any row violates the condition. expect_all/expect_all_or_drop/expect_all_or_fail apply multiple named rules at once.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: A common trap is thinking plain expect drops rows, it only reports; drop and fail take action.

intermediateQuestions.question: How does APPLY CHANGES INTO implement SCD Type 2 from a CDC feed?
intermediateQuestions.answer: You declare a target streaming table and call apply_changes with keys, a sequence_by column, optional apply_as_deletes, and stored_as_scd_type=2. DLT orders changes by the sequence column (handling out-of-order records), applies inserts/updates/deletes, and maintains validity columns (__START_AT/__END_AT) so each key keeps historical versions with the current one left open.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Emphasize ordering via a monotonic sequence and automatic history/validity maintenance.

advancedQuestions.question: How does DLT decide whether a materialized view is refreshed incrementally or fully recomputed, and why does it matter?
advancedQuestions.answer: DLT's Enzyme engine analyzes the query and available change data from upstream Delta tables. If the transformation is incrementalizable (e.g., appends into a groupBy aggregation), it computes only the delta and merges results; if the query pattern, non-determinism, or source changes make incremental unsafe, it falls back to a full recompute. It matters because incremental refresh dramatically lowers cost and latency for gold aggregates, so writing incremental-friendly queries and running on serverless (where Enzyme is available) is a real optimization lever.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Strong answers connect Enzyme, query determinism, cost/latency impact, and how to keep queries incremental-friendly.

advancedQuestions.question: Walk through how DLT guarantees exactly-once, consistent results across failures in a streaming pipeline.
advancedQuestions.answer: Streaming tables run on Structured Streaming with DLT-managed checkpoints that track source offsets, and writes go to Delta tables using ACID transactions so each micro-batch commits atomically. On failure, the update rolls back at the dataset level and, in production mode, retries from the last committed offset, reprocessing only uncommitted data. APPLY CHANGES ordering and idempotent Delta writes ensure retries never duplicate rows, yielding exactly-once end-to-end for supported sources.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Cover managed checkpoints/offsets, Delta ACID atomic commits, dataset-level rollback, production-mode retries, and idempotency.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your gold daily-revenue materialized view is recomputing fully every run and costing too much, even though only a few new orders arrive each hour. How do you diagnose and fix it?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Confirm it is a materialized view and that Enzyme can incrementalize it: check the event log/pipeline UI for full-recompute indicators, verify the upstream is a Delta source producing change data, check for non-deterministic functions or unsupported patterns that block incremental refresh, and confirm you are on serverless where Enzyme is available.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Move the pipeline to serverless so Enzyme incremental refresh is available, ensure the upstream silver is an append-friendly Delta streaming table, rewrite the aggregate to be deterministic and incrementalizable (simple SUM/COUNT group-bys), remove non-deterministic UDFs/functions, and verify via the event log that subsequent refreshes process only the delta rather than a full scan. Consider triggered execution to align compute with the hourly cadence.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a DLT-based medallion pipeline that ingests high-volume clickstream and a CDC customer feed, enforces data quality, maintains a Type 2 customer dimension, and serves hourly engagement metrics to BI with strong governance and controlled cost.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Bronze: Auto Loader streaming tables for clickstream (cloudFiles) and a streaming table over the CDC Delta feed, with expect tags for missing IDs. Silver: cleansed clickstream streaming table using expect_all_or_drop and expect_or_fail for invariants, plus APPLY CHANGES INTO to build customers_scd2 (keys, sequence_by, deletes). Gold: materialized view joining engagement to current customer rows, aggregated hourly, refreshed incrementally by Enzyme. Target Unity Catalog catalog.schema, run in production mode on serverless with enhanced autoscaling, triggered hourly.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Triggered vs. continuous trades cost for latency; expect_or_fail protects invariants but risks halting on upstream regressions; serverless simplifies ops and enables Enzyme but is usage-billed; SCD Type 2 preserves history at higher storage cost than Type 1.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Enhanced autoscaling handles clickstream bursts by adding/removing executors on backlog; Auto Loader scales file discovery; Enzyme keeps gold refresh cheap as data grows; partition/liquid-cluster gold serving tables and enable Photon for fast BI reads. Scale horizontally by splitting domains into separate pipelines if the DAG grows large.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Delta Live Tables (Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines) is a declarative ETL framework where you define streaming tables and materialized views with data-quality expectations, and DLT manages the dependency DAG, incremental processing, checkpoints, CDC/SCD, and observability.
keyConcepts: Declarative: you define datasets and queries; DLT infers the DAG and manages execution.
Streaming table = incremental append/ingest; materialized view = incrementally refreshed aggregation.
Expectations: expect (track), expect_or_drop (filter), expect_or_fail (halt); expect_all for groups.
APPLY CHANGES INTO handles CDC and SCD Type 1/2 with keys + sequence_by.
Event log = observability for flow progress, expectation metrics, and lineage.
formulas: Streaming semantics: exactly-once = managed checkpoint (offsets) + Delta ACID atomic commit
Cost intuition: triggered (compute only when running) < continuous (always-on); serverless bills per use
commands: @dlt.table / @dlt.view  # Python: declare a materialized/streaming table or a view
dlt.read_stream("upstream") / dlt.read("upstream")  # streaming vs batch dependency
CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE t AS SELECT ... FROM STREAM read_files(...);
CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW mv AS SELECT ... GROUP BY ...;
APPLY CHANGES INTO live.t FROM STREAM(live.cdc) KEYS (id) SEQUENCE BY seq STORED AS SCD TYPE 2;
interviewPoints: Declarative (WHAT) vs. imperative Structured Streaming (HOW); DLT manages the DAG and checkpoints.
Streaming table vs. materialized view: know when each is correct.
Three expectation actions; plain expect only tracks, it does not drop.
APPLY CHANGES INTO for CDC/SCD; needs a monotonic sequence column.
Development vs. production mode; triggered vs. continuous; enhanced autoscaling; serverless + Enzyme.
Event log is the observability and data-quality metrics source; publish to Unity Catalog for governance.
quickNotes: Reference upstream datasets via dlt.read/dlt.read_stream (or STREAM()/live.) so DLT builds the DAG.
Bronze thin, silver conform + quality, gold aggregate; keep transforms deterministic/idempotent.
Use expect_or_drop with a quarantine table for triage; reserve expect_or_fail for hard invariants.
Enzyme incrementally refreshes materialized views on serverless; keep queries incremental-friendly.
Set target catalog.schema (Unity Catalog); run production pipelines in production mode with autoscaling.

keyTakeaways: Delta Live Tables (Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines) is a declarative ETL framework: you define streaming tables, materialized views, and expectations, and DLT infers the dependency DAG and manages checkpoints, incremental processing, retries, and observability.

Pick dataset types deliberately, streaming tables (via spark.readStream / dlt.read_stream) for append-heavy ingestion and materialized views (via dlt.read + aggregation, refreshed incrementally by Enzyme) for aggregations across the bronze/silver/gold medallion layers.

Data quality is first-class via expectations: expect tracks, expect_or_drop filters/quarantines, and expect_or_fail halts the update, with per-expectation metrics emitted to the DLT event log for monitoring and alerting.

APPLY CHANGES INTO (dlt.apply_changes) declaratively handles CDC and SCD Type 1/2 using key and monotonic sequence columns, replacing fragile hand-written MERGE-and-order logic and correctly handling out-of-order records and deletes.

For production, target Unity Catalog, run in production mode with enhanced autoscaling (or serverless), choose triggered vs. continuous by SLA, and rely on the event log and Delta ACID/managed checkpoints for exactly-once, governed, observable pipelines.
